title: Supply & Demand
description: How prices emerge from buyers meeting sellers

concepts.title: The Demand Curve
concepts.contentHtml:
At its core, demand is a relationship: how much of a good buyers want at each possible price.

The law of demand says that — holding everything else constant — quantity demanded falls as price rises. Plot price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal, and you get a curve sloping down and to the right.

Two reasons it slopes down. The substitution effect: when coffee gets expensive, buyers switch to tea. The income effect: when prices rise, your real purchasing power falls, so you buy less of most things.

concepts.title: The Supply Curve
concepts.contentHtml:
Supply is the mirror image: how much sellers want to produce at each price.

The law of supply says quantity supplied rises with price. Higher prices cover higher marginal costs, attract new entrants, and pull resources away from other uses. The supply curve slopes up and to the right.

This holds in the short run when capacity is fixed. In the long run, supply tends to be more elastic — firms can build factories, hire workers, plant more crops.

concepts.title: Market Equilibrium
concepts.contentHtml:
Where the demand and supply curves intersect, you get the equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q*.

At P*, the amount buyers want exactly equals the amount sellers want to provide. There's no shortage and no surplus — the market clears.

Equilibrium isn't permanent — it's the rest point given current conditions. Change anything (tastes, costs, incomes, the weather) and the curves shift, producing a new equilibrium.

concepts.title: Shifts vs Movements
concepts.contentHtml:
This is the distinction that trips people up. There are two different kinds of change.

A movement along the curve happens when price itself changes. Same curve, different point on it.

A shift of the curve happens when something other than price changes — income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, number of buyers/sellers, input costs, technology. The whole curve moves left or right.

Rule of thumb: if price moved, you moved along. If anything else moved, the curve shifted.

concepts.title: Surplus, Shortage & Price Adjustment
concepts.contentHtml:
What if the price is wrong?

Above equilibrium, sellers want to sell more than buyers want to buy. That's a surplus — unsold inventory piles up. Sellers cut prices to move it. Price falls toward P*.

Below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers will provide. That's a shortage — empty shelves, queues, black markets. Sellers raise prices. Price rises toward P*.

This is why economists treat the equilibrium as a kind of attractor: deviations create pressure that pushes price back. Price ceilings (rent control) and price floors (minimum wage) lock prices off equilibrium and produce persistent shortages or surpluses.

title: Elasticity
description: How responsive quantity is to price, income, and other prices

concepts.title: Price Elasticity of Demand
concepts.contentHtml:
Knowing demand slopes down isn't enough — we want to know how steeply. Price elasticity of demand measures the percentage change in quantity demanded for a 1% change in price.

It's a unitless ratio, which is the whole point: it lets you compare responsiveness across goods regardless of whether they're sold by the kilo, the litre, or the dozen.

By convention, since the relationship is negative, we usually report the absolute value. An elasticity of 2 means a 1% price increase causes a 2% drop in quantity.

concepts.title: Elastic vs Inelastic
concepts.contentHtml:
The magic number is 1.

If |ε| > 1, demand is elastic — buyers respond strongly to price. Luxury goods, brand-name products, things with close substitutes.

If |ε| < 1, demand is inelastic — buyers barely react. Insulin, gasoline in the short run, addictive goods, cheap necessities.

If |ε| = 1, demand is unit elastic — quantity changes proportionally with price.

The two extremes: perfectly inelastic (vertical curve, ε = 0 — buyers will pay anything) and perfectly elastic (horizontal curve, ε = ∞ — any price increase loses all sales). Real goods sit between.

concepts.title: What Determines Elasticity?
concepts.contentHtml:
Four big drivers:

1. Substitutes. The more close substitutes, the more elastic. Coke is elastic (Pepsi exists). Salt is inelastic (no real substitute, and you barely use any).

2. Necessity vs luxury. Necessities are inelastic, luxuries are elastic.

3. Share of budget. Goods that take up a big slice of income (housing, cars) tend to be more elastic, because buyers shop hard. Pencils are inelastic.

4. Time horizon. Demand is more elastic in the long run. Gasoline is inelastic this week — you still need to drive to work — but elastic over a decade as people buy fuel-efficient cars or move closer to work.

concepts.title: Income & Cross-Price Elasticity
concepts.contentHtml:
Elasticity isn't only about own-price.

Income elasticity measures how demand responds to income changes. If it's positive, the good is normal (most things). If greater than 1, it's a luxury. If negative, it's an inferior good — buyers shift away as they get richer (instant noodles, used cars, intercity buses).

Cross-price elasticity measures how good A's quantity responds to good B's price. Positive: A and B are substitutes (tea and coffee). Negative: complements (printers and ink). Zero: unrelated.

concepts.title: Why Elasticity Matters: Tax Incidence & Revenue
concepts.contentHtml:
Elasticity isn't an academic curiosity — it determines who pays.

Tax incidence: when a tax is levied, the side of the market that's more inelastic bears more of it. Cigarette demand is inelastic, so smokers absorb most of cigarette taxes regardless of who legally pays. Land supply is perfectly inelastic, so a land tax falls entirely on landowners — Henry George's famous insight.

Revenue: raising the price of an inelastic good increases total revenue (quantity barely falls). Raising the price of an elastic good decreases it (quantity falls faster than price rises). This is why monopolies set prices in the elastic region and why cartels fail when substitutes appear.

title: Consumer Choice & Utility
description: Indifference curves, budget constraints, and the marginal calculus of preference

concepts.title: Utility & Marginal Utility
concepts.contentHtml:
Utility is the economist's word for satisfaction — a numerical stand-in for how much a consumer values a bundle of goods. We don't claim it's measurable in lab units; we just need it to rank bundles consistently.

Marginal utility is the extra utility from one more unit. The first slice of pizza is wonderful; the fifth, less so; the tenth might make you sick.

This is the law of diminishing marginal utility — and it's the deep reason demand curves slope down. As you consume more, each additional unit is worth less to you, so you'll only buy more if the price drops.

concepts.title: Indifference Curves
concepts.contentHtml:
An indifference curve shows all bundles of two goods that give the consumer the same utility. The consumer is — by definition — indifferent between any two points on the same curve.

Three properties matter. They slope downward: more of one means less of the other to stay equally happy. They are convex: variety beats extremes — you'd trade a lot of pizza for the first beer but not for the tenth. They don't cross: that would be a logical contradiction.

The slope of an indifference curve is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS) — how much of Y you'll give up for one more X while staying equally well off. It equals the ratio of marginal utilities.

concepts.title: The Budget Constraint
concepts.contentHtml:
Wants are infinite; budgets aren't. The budget constraint draws the line.

If income is I and prices are P_x and P_y, you can afford any bundle (x, y) such that P_x·x + P_y·y ≤ I. Plotted on the same axes as indifference curves, it's a downward-sloping straight line. Its slope is −P_x/P_y — the market rate at which you can trade Y for X.

Two things shift the budget line. Income changes shift it parallel — outward when richer, inward when poorer. A price change rotates it — only the affected intercept moves.

concepts.title: Optimal Choice: Tangency
concepts.contentHtml:
Put indifference curves and the budget line on one diagram. Where does the consumer end up?

On the highest indifference curve they can afford — which is where an indifference curve is just tangent to the budget line. Anywhere else, they could move along the budget and reach a higher curve.

At tangency, the slopes are equal: MRS = P_x/P_y. The internal trade-off (how much Y you'd give up for X) matches the external trade-off (how much you must give up). Equivalently: the marginal utility per dollar is equal across all goods. If a dollar of pizza gave more utility than a dollar of beer, you'd shift spending until the margins equalized.

concepts.title: Substitution & Income Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
When a price changes, the optimal bundle shifts for two reasons.

The substitution effect: with X cheaper relative to Y, you swap toward X — even if your real income stayed the same. This is the pure relative price effect, and it always points toward the now-cheaper good.

The income effect: a lower P_x means your fixed money income now buys more — your real income rose. You consume more of normal goods, less of inferior goods.

Add the two together and you get the total response. For nearly every good, both push the same way and demand falls when price rises. Rare exception: Giffen goods — inferior goods so dominant in the budget that the income effect overwhelms substitution, producing an upward-sloping demand curve. Mostly a textbook curiosity: the famous 19th-century Irish potato case is disputed, but Jensen and Miller (2008) found Giffen behavior for rice and wheat among poor households in Hunan and Gansu, China.

title: Producer Theory & Costs
description: Production functions, marginal cost, returns to scale, the firm's supply curve

concepts.title: The Production Function
concepts.contentHtml:
A firm turns inputs into outputs. The production function Q = f(L, K, …) is the recipe — the maximum output achievable from given quantities of labor L, capital K, and other inputs.

It's the engineering side of the firm, not the financial one. Costs come later. First we ask: given technology, what's possible?

The famous Cobb-Douglas form, Q = A·L^α·K^β, is a workhorse — flexible enough to capture most cases, simple enough to differentiate by hand.
mathExpressions: Q = f(L, K), \quad Q = A L^{\alpha} K^{\beta}

concepts.title: Marginal Product & Diminishing Returns
concepts.contentHtml:
The marginal product of an input is the extra output from one more unit, holding other inputs fixed.

The law of diminishing marginal returns: as you add more of one input to a fixed amount of another, the marginal product eventually falls. One cook in a kitchen produces a lot. Two cooks produce more, but not double. Ten cooks step on each other.

Crucially, this is a short-run phenomenon — it only applies when something else is fixed. In the long run, you can scale all inputs together, and the rules change (see returns to scale).

concepts.title: Costs: Fixed, Variable, Total
concepts.contentHtml:
In the short run, costs split into two:

Fixed costs (FC) don't depend on output — rent, insurance, debt service. You pay them whether you produce zero or a million units.

Variable costs (VC) rise with output — materials, hourly labor, electricity.

Total cost is TC = FC + VC. From these we get the per-unit measures: average cost AC = TC/Q, average variable cost AVC = VC/Q, average fixed cost AFC = FC/Q (which always falls — fixed costs spread over more units).

concepts.title: Marginal Cost & the Cost Curves
concepts.contentHtml:
The most important cost concept is marginal cost — the cost of producing one more unit. It comes from variable cost (fixed costs are already sunk).

MC typically falls at first (specialization, learning) then rises (diminishing returns kick in). The result: a U-shaped curve.

A geometric fact worth memorizing: MC cuts AC and AVC at their minimums. When marginal is below average, average falls; when marginal is above, average rises. Same logic as test scores — your next exam pulls your average up only if it's higher than your current average.

concepts.title: Returns to Scale
concepts.contentHtml:
What happens if you double everything — labor, capital, land, all inputs?

Constant returns to scale: output exactly doubles. Most production replicates cleanly at this scale.

Increasing returns to scale: output more than doubles. Sources: specialization, network effects, fixed costs spread thin, geometry (a tank's volume grows faster than its surface area). Drives the rise of large firms.

Decreasing returns to scale: output less than doubles. Coordination breaks down, management gets stretched, congestion sets in. Why no firm grows forever.

Note: returns to scale is a long-run concept (everything varies). Diminishing marginal returns is short-run (one input fixed). Don't confuse them.

concepts.title: Profit Maximization & the Firm's Supply Curve
concepts.contentHtml:
How much should a firm produce? The rule that runs all of microeconomics:

Produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. If MR > MC, the next unit adds more revenue than cost — make it. If MR < MC, you're losing on the margin — cut back.

For a competitive firm, price is given by the market, so MR = P. The firm produces where P = MC. That makes the upward-sloping part of the MC curve the firm's supply curve — directly answering 'how much will it produce at each price?'

One caveat: the firm only produces if price covers AVC. Below that, it can't even pay its workers, and shutting down (eating only the fixed cost) is better than producing.

title: Market Structures
description: Perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition

concepts.title: Perfect Competition
concepts.contentHtml:
Perfect competition is the textbook benchmark — and almost a fiction. Its assumptions: many small firms, identical products, free entry and exit, perfect information, no transport or transaction costs.

The consequence: every firm is a price taker. The market sets P; the firm just decides Q. Its demand curve is horizontal at the market price.

In the long run, free entry drives economic profit to zero. Any profit attracts entrants, supply expands, price falls until just covering costs. The result: P = MC = minimum AC. Allocatively and productively efficient — and the standard against which all other structures are judged.

concepts.title: Monopoly
concepts.contentHtml:
A monopoly is a single seller facing the entire market demand curve — which slopes down. To sell more, the monopolist must drop the price, and not just on the marginal unit but on every unit.

This makes marginal revenue lie below price. The profit-maximizing rule MR = MC then gives a quantity below the competitive level and a price above marginal cost.

Result: the monopolist captures producer surplus that would have been consumer surplus, plus a chunk of mutually beneficial trades simply doesn't happen — the deadweight loss. Sources of monopoly: patents, network effects, control of a key input, regulatory protection, natural monopoly (very high fixed costs, like pipelines).

concepts.title: Monopolistic Competition
concepts.contentHtml:
Most real markets sit between perfect competition and monopoly. Monopolistic competition describes the most common case: many firms, free entry, but differentiated products.

Restaurants, clothing brands, hairdressers, software apps. Each firm has a downward-sloping demand curve (because its product isn't identical to rivals') but limited pricing power (because substitutes are close).

Long-run outcome: free entry drives profit to zero, but firms produce below minimum AC — there's excess capacity, the price of variety. Most economists view this as a fair trade: real consumers value variety, even if it costs some efficiency.

concepts.title: Oligopoly & Strategic Interaction
concepts.contentHtml:
Oligopoly means a few firms, each big enough that its actions move the market. Airlines, telecom, mobile OS, soda. Now the key word is strategic: each firm must anticipate what the others will do.

Two classical models. Cournot: firms simultaneously choose quantities, each best-responding to expected rival output. The Nash equilibrium gives a price and quantity between monopoly and competition.

Bertrand: firms simultaneously choose prices. Surprisingly, with identical products and constant marginal cost, two firms is enough to drive price down to MC — the Bertrand paradox.

Real oligopolies often try to coordinate (cartels, OPEC), but cooperation is fragile because each member has a strong incentive to cheat — a classic prisoner's dilemma. Game theory is the natural language here.

concepts.title: Comparing Outcomes
concepts.contentHtml:
Lining up the four structures by efficiency (most to least):

Perfect competition: P = MC. No deadweight loss. Allocative and productive efficiency. Zero economic profit in the long run.

Monopolistic competition: P > MC slightly. Small deadweight loss, excess capacity from variety. Zero profit long-run.

Oligopoly: P > MC, depends on strategic behavior. Outcomes range from near-competitive (Bertrand) to near-monopoly (collusion).

Monopoly: P >> MC. Largest deadweight loss. Persistent positive profit unless eroded by entry, regulation, or technological disruption.

This ranking explains why antitrust law targets monopolization and price-fixing: deviations from competition have measurable welfare costs.

title: Externalities & Market Failure
description: When prices don't reflect true social costs — pollution, public goods, asymmetric info

concepts.title: Externalities
concepts.contentHtml:
Markets work when the people making the decision bear all the costs and reap all the benefits. An externality is what happens when they don't — when an action spills costs or benefits onto third parties.

Negative externalities: pollution, traffic congestion, second-hand smoke, antibiotic overuse. The polluter's private cost is below the social cost, so they over-produce.

Positive externalities: vaccinations, education, basic research, well-maintained gardens. Private benefit is below social benefit, so the activity is under-provided.

Either way, the unfettered market quantity isn't socially optimal — there's a wedge between private and social marginal calculus. Closing it is the central problem of welfare economics.

concepts.title: Coase Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Ronald Coase's striking insight: if property rights are clearly defined and bargaining is costless, parties can negotiate to the efficient outcome regardless of who initially holds the right.

Classic example: a factory pollutes; nearby residents are harmed. Whether the residents have a right to clean air (and the factory pays them to pollute) or the factory has a right to pollute (and residents pay them to stop), efficient pollution levels emerge from bargaining. The distribution differs, but the quantity doesn't.

The catch is in the assumption: transaction costs are real. Many parties, asymmetric information, hold-out problems, and enforcement costs can all block the deal. Coase didn't claim externalities are non-problems; he claimed that market failure isn't automatic — you need to ask why bargaining can't fix it. Often the honest answer is too many people, and that's where policy comes in.

concepts.title: Pigouvian Taxes & Subsidies
concepts.contentHtml:
Arthur Pigou's policy answer: tax negative externalities, subsidize positive ones — at a rate equal to the marginal external effect.

A Pigouvian tax raises the polluter's private cost to match the social cost. They internalize what they used to externalize. Quantity falls to the social optimum, and the government collects revenue. Using that revenue to cut other distorting taxes is the hoped-for 'double dividend'.

A Pigouvian subsidy works the other way for positive externalities — vaccination subsidies, R&D credits, education funding.

Carbon taxes are the canonical modern Pigouvian tax. They price the climate damage of each ton of CO₂. Cap-and-trade systems achieve a similar outcome via quantity rather than price — economists generally view both as preferable to direct regulation, which lacks the flexibility of letting markets find the cheapest abatement.
mathExpressions: t^* = MEC \text{ at the social optimum}

concepts.title: Public Goods
concepts.contentHtml:
A public good has two unusual properties:

Non-rival: one person's consumption doesn't reduce what's available to others. A streetlight illuminates the whole street; my looking at it doesn't dim it for you.

Non-excludable: you can't easily prevent non-payers from benefiting. Once national defense exists, every citizen is protected.

The market under-provides public goods because of the free rider problem: rational individuals wait for someone else to pay. Examples: lighthouses, basic research, clean air, herd immunity, open-source software.

Standard fix: government provision financed by taxes. But not all under-provision needs the state — Elinor Ostrom showed that communities often self-govern common-pool resources (a related but distinct case where goods are rival but non-excludable).

concepts.title: Asymmetric Information
concepts.contentHtml:
Markets assume both sides know what they're trading. When they don't, things break in two ways.

Adverse selection — hidden information before the deal. Akerlof's lemons: used cars. Sellers know quality, buyers don't. Buyers offer the average price; good-car owners walk away; only lemons remain; the price falls further; the market unravels. Same logic explains why insurance markets struggle — the sickest most want coverage.

Moral hazard — hidden action after the deal. Once insured, you're more careless with your bike. Once bailed out, banks take more risk. The agent's incentives no longer match the principal's.

Fixes vary: signaling (warranties, education credentials), screening (insurance questionnaires, deductibles), reputation, regulation, and contracts that tie pay to outcomes. Spence, Akerlof, and Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel for working this out.
